answer: Agents that monitor a lagoon, trade pigment, or manage a grove settle payments on a ledger where voting power is proportional to locked collateral. Splitting one stake among a thousand identities gives an attacker no extra voting power: controlling a majority requires acquiring and locking a majority of the stake. Signing conflicting ledger histories produces verifiable evidence that burns the offending stake, making that attack costly even if the identities are disposable.
